administering_agency: California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA); transitioning to Housing Development and Finance Committee (HDFC) under the California Housing and Homelessness Agency
typical_award_size: 2026 round: $63M in subsidy loans to 13 developments (1,768 units); funded by 15% of SB 2 Building Homes and Jobs Act revenue. Per project: lesser of $6M, $50,000 per MIP-regulated unit ($60,000 in High or Highest Resource areas), or 50% of the CalHFA permanent loan. Sponsor limited to one award per year; no county may receive more than 25% of annual funds; age-restricted projects capped at 25%.
affordability_requirement: New construction, 4% credits with income averaging; at least 51% LIHTC units. MIP regulatory agreement (55 years): 30% of units at or below 50% AMI (including 10% at or below 30% AMI), 10% of units at 60% to 80% AMI averaging 70%, remaining units at or below 120% AMI; spread between lowest and highest targets at least 40 points; average affordability no more than 60% AMI. Rents at least 10% below market.
layering_notes: Must use CalHFA Conduit Issuer Program for construction bonds and CalHFA Tax-Exempt Permanent Loan (minimum $5M perm loan, 1.15x DSCR). Draws on the $100M enhanced state credit MIP set-aside at CTCAC and the $310M State-funded Mixed Income bond set-aside at CDLAC, so MIP projects compete for bonds outside the geographic pools. Cannot be combined with 9% credits. 3% simple interest, residual receipts (50% of surplus cash), coterminous with perm loan, 1% loan fee. Term sheet is silent on prevailing wage; a 3% subordinate loan may fit the Labor Code 1720(c)(6)(E) below-market-loan exemption if 40% of units are restricted at 80% AMI for 20 years, but confirm with counsel. Governor's reorganization moves MIP into HDFC with HCD programs for a unified application.

program_name: Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF), Sonoma County Housing Successor
administering_agency: Sonoma County Community Development Commission as housing successor to the former County redevelopment agency
typical_award_size: Up to $250,000 per year for homeless prevention and rapid rehousing services (FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27 NOFAs). Fund balance available for all uses $2,509,338 at June 30, 2025; loans receivable $31.2M; FY 2024-25 expenditures $3.84M. Not currently offered for development.
affordability_requirement: Community Redevelopment Law housing provisions (very low and low income); current awards are homeless services, not capital.
layering_notes: Included so the fund is not mistaken for a development source: the County keeps LMIHAF for services and the former RDA Reinvestment and Revitalization money flows into CFH instead. Loan repayments from legacy RDA projects replenish the fund and could be redirected to capital in future years.

program_name: County conduit multifamily housing revenue bonds (none; CMFA used in Napa County)
administering_agency: Napa County (not an active conduit issuer); California Municipal Finance Authority used instead
typical_award_size: No county issuance program found. Recent Napa County deals used CMFA: Napa Park Homes, City of Napa, 140 units acquisition-rehab, $43,575,000 (2026); St. Anton Partners refinancing, City of Napa, $20,135,000; BRIDGE Housing, Calistoga and St. Helena, $20,544,520.
affordability_requirement: Per CDLAC: at least 20% of units at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI, 55-year regulatory agreement.
layering_notes: Negative finding recorded so later passes do not search again. 4% deals in Napa pair CMFA bonds with CTCAC credits, County Affordable Housing Fund or City of Napa funds, and HCD programs (Manzanita used AHSC, NHTF and HOME). Conduit bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage; the deal's public subordinate loans usually do.

program_name: Launchpad workforce housing incentive, eastern Placer County (Transient Occupancy Tax through the TOT-TBID Dollars at Work program)
administering_agency: Placer County Executive Office, Economic Development and Housing (Timothy Cussen, Housing Specialist); Tahoe City office 775 North Lake Boulevard; funding recommended by the North Tahoe Community Alliance (NTCA) TOT-TBID Dollars at Work program
typical_award_size: $200,000 per unit for category one (condos, townhomes, multifamily units and conversions of non-residential or non-code-compliant space; single-family homes are not eligible), $125,000 per ADU and $50,000 per SRO unit, paid at completion once the 55-year workforce Use Deed Restriction is recorded. Funding: $1,000,000 inaugural NOFA LP-001 (April 2025) reserved $725,000 for two Kings Beach projects (Steelhead Avenue Cottage Court, 3 tiny homes, $600,000; accessible ADU, $125,000). The February 2026 NOFA LP-002 offered $3,275,000 ($3,000,000 of new TOT approved February 3, 2026 plus $275,000 carryover), drew 12 applications ($10,550,000 requested) and reserved $3,250,000 for four projects: Lake Forest Multifamily (12 studios, Tahoe City, $2,400,000), Dollar Hill Tiny Homes (3 units, $600,000) and two tiny home ADUs ($125,000 each).
affordability_requirement: Units must be in unincorporated eastern Placer County within the Tahoe Truckee Unified School District boundary, outside avalanche hazard areas, with entitlements in place or allowed by right. A 55-year Use Deed Restriction (restarting on each transfer) requires occupancy as a primary residence by a qualified household with a local worker employed within the TTUSD area; no income limit or sales price cap. Units used to meet the Affordable Housing and Employee Accommodation Ordinance are ineligible.
layering_notes: placer.ca.gov (including DocumentCenter PDFs) sits behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06; Board items were read from the County's GovDelivery agenda attachments (content.govdelivery.com/attachments/CAPLACER), the Legistar client 'placerca', state records and news coverage. Launchpad is a per-unit grant rather than a loan and is sized for small infill projects in Kings Beach, Tahoe City and the North Shore; a 10-unit workforce project could draw $2 million, which is meaningful against TRPA coverage and construction costs in the Basin. It pays only at completion, so it is bridge-financed. The workforce (not income) restriction means it does not fit LIHTC deals directly but can fund unrestricted middle-income units in a mixed-income project. TOT funds are County funds, so prevailing wage status is unclear under Labor Code 1720; confirm with the County. North Lake Tahoe TOT also funds the Workforce Housing Preservation Program and the Dollar Creek Crossing effort.

program_name: Project-Based Vouchers, Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz
administering_agency: Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz (2160 41st Avenue, Capitola; (831) 454-9455; PBV RFP contact Eric Johnson, Senior Analyst)
typical_award_size: 823 PBVs in 33 developments as of February 2025 (El Centro 44, St. Stephens Senior 39, Water Street 33, Pippin Orchards 31, Resetar 52 and others) plus commitments to projects in development including Veterans Village (15). PBVs are awarded through a competitive RFP; the Fall 2024 RFP (open Oct 15 to Nov 18, 2024) offered up to 90 HCV and 15 VASH vouchers. HACSC planned two rounds a year timed to CTCAC, but the Spring-Summer 2025 RFP was cancelled because of federal funding uncertainty and no RFP has been reissued as of November 2026. Fall 2024 scoring: 200 base points (project type 45, HCV waiting list opportunities 25, poverty deconcentration 10, additional non-PBV affordable units 50, location 14, experience 6, readiness 15, community engagement 5, financial feasibility 30) plus up to 10 bonus points for supportive services or resident benefits; threshold 125 points for new construction and 120 for existing housing.
affordability_requirement: Tenants pay 30% of income; HCV waiting list, site-based lists or Coordinated Entry referrals; HACSC administers special purpose vouchers (Mainstream, FUP, VASH) that can be project-based.
layering_notes: Santa Cruz County housing programs sit in the Community Development and Infrastructure Department (CDI) Planning Division, Housing Section (HousingProgramsInfo@santacruzcountyCA.gov, (831) 454-2332), which runs the Measure J inclusionary program, the Affordable Housing Impact Fee, LMIHAF, PLHA and the County housing NOFA; the Human Services Department's Housing for Health Division (H4H, the CoC CA-508 lead) runs HHAP, Homekey and homeless programs; Behavioral Health holds BHSA; and the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz (HACSC) supplies vouchers. The County is a non-entitlement jurisdiction for CDBG and HOME. County programs apply only to the unincorporated area (about half the population); Santa Cruz, Watsonville, Capitola and Scotts Valley run their own programs (Pass 3). cdi.santacruzcountyca.gov, santacruzcountyca.gov PDFs, santacruzhealth.org and housingforhealthpartnership.org open normally; the Board's IQM2 portal (santacruzcountyca.iqm2.com) renders by script and could not be listed, so Board items were taken from NOFA appendices and press coverage. PBVs have been the operating subsidy in nearly every recent Santa Cruz County affordable deal; with the RFP paused since spring 2025, developers are turning to BHSA and HHAP subsidies and to CoC rental assistance. Source is the HACSC request for proposals page (RFP status); project list from the February 2025 in-service PBV list and selection rules from the 2022 owner guidance.

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act Integrated Plan FY 2026-29 and Behavioral Health Bridge Housing (Hotel Casa Grande)
typical_award_size: Madera County (population about 160,000) is eligible for the small-county housing interventions exemption; its FY 2026-29 Integrated Plan and any exemption or transfer request could not be read (County website blocked). Known housing activity: Behavioral Health Bridge Housing at the Hotel Casa Grande (37 units) with a three-year, $6.9 million supportive services contract to RH Community Builders approved August 2024; a May 2026 two-year shared-housing agreement with Madera Rescue Mission reserving 34 beds (not to exceed $1,212,576); BHCIP Round 5 award of $24,989,161 (July 2023) for a youth and adult crisis stabilization unit and sobering center (facility, not housing).
affordability_requirement: BHSA eligible adults and youth with serious mental illness or substance use disorder.
layering_notes: Madera County is a small non-entitlement county: the Community and Economic Development Department (planning, state CDBG and HOME applications) and Behavioral Health Services (BHSA, bridge housing) are the only County housing actors, the Housing Authority of the City of Madera (HACM) is the PHA for the county, and the Fresno Madera Continuum of Care (CA-514, led by Fresno County) handles HHAP and CoC funds. There is no County housing trust fund, NOFA, inclusionary ordinance or impact fee waiver program. The City of Madera is a separate CDBG and HOME entitlement with its own PLHA plan (Pass 3). maderacounty.com blocks automated access (403 on pages and documents), the PrimeGov and IQM2 portals returned no 2026 meetings, and Board agendas were read from PDFs mirrored on maderacountywater.com; other sources were HCD allocation tables, maderaha.org, zoneomics (County Code Title 18), CEQAnet and press coverage. Confirmation needed: BHSA housing dollars, exemption status and any PSH capital plans. Madera's pattern is motel-based bridge housing and contracted beds rather than capital; a developer would be looking at an operating or master-lease contract. Source is the County MHSA/BHSA page (blocked to automated access); the bridge housing and BHCIP details come from the Madera Tribune (July 9, 2023) and Board meeting summaries.

program_name: Western Nevada County Regional Housing Trust Fund (WNCRHTF) gap loans
administering_agency: Nevada County Housing and Community Services Department (with City of Grass Valley and Nevada City)
typical_award_size: Formed July 14, 2020 (Resolutions 20-315, 20-316, 20-317) by the County, Grass Valley and Nevada City, capitalized with PLHA, a state Local Housing Trust Fund (LHTF) matching grant awarded February 3, 2021, HHSA Intergovernmental Transfer funds, ARPA and a $1 million General Fund commitment repurposed as match in 2025. Awards to date: Cashin's Field (51 units, Nevada City, Resolution 21-116 loan, completed January 2023); Lone Oak Senior Apartments II (31 units, Penn Valley, Pacific West Communities) $1,024,775 under RFP 3 (Resolution 23-227, May 23, 2023) plus $1,281,373 (Resolution 25-167, May 13, 2025) for a $2,306,128 loan approved May 19, 2026 (Resolution 26-196); Habitat for Humanity Ventana Sierra (owner-occupied, May 2023 RFP).
affordability_requirement: Low income rental or owner-occupied housing; the Lone Oak II loan is an unsecured deferred loan repaid from residual receipts with affordability tied to the TCAC regulatory agreement. LHTF rules (lower income, 55-year rental covenants, 3% simple maximum) apply to the state-matched share.
layering_notes: Nevada County's Housing and Community Services Department (HCS, Tyler Barrington, Director, 950 Maidu Ave, Nevada City, 530-265-1645, Housing@nevadacountyca.gov) sits inside the Health and Human Services Agency and administers the Western Nevada County Regional Housing Trust Fund, PLHA (as delegated applicant for Grass Valley and Nevada City), state HOME and CDBG awards, the MORE mobile home program and the new Down Payment Assistance Program; the Behavioral Health and Homelessness Department (Cari Yardley, Director) holds Homekey+, BHSA and the Truckee Navigation Center; HHAP is administered by the Homeless Resource Council of the Sierras as the CoC CA-531 lead; and the Regional Housing Authority (Sutter, Nevada, Yuba, Colusa and Lake counties, Yuba City) supplies vouchers. Grass Valley, Nevada City and Truckee run their own programs (Pass 3). The County has no inclusionary ordinance, no housing impact fee and no affordable housing fee waiver program; the only land use incentive is the state density bonus ordinance. nevadacountyca.gov opens directly and the Legistar web API client 'nevco' exposes staff reports and attachments at legistar.granicus.com/nevco/attachments/. The trust fund is the County's only local gap source and has been used as the TCAC local contribution that moved Lone Oak II from unfunded to a December 2025 4% award. Expect small amounts ($1 million to $2.3 million) and a Board resolution for each loan. Pair with state HOME (Lone Oak II received $11,041,628) and CMFA or CSCDA conduit bonds. Future awards are likely to come as direct PLHA loans scored jointly with the two cities instead of trust fund loans.

program_name: Folsom legacy housing funds: Oaks at Willow Springs inclusionary fund (Fund 274) and former redevelopment bond proceeds (Fund 280)
administering_agency: City of Folsom Community Development Department, Housing Services
typical_award_size: Largely spent. Fund 274 held $25,672 at June 30, 2025 from a 2006 $3.1M inclusionary payment ($2.7M went to the Granite City Apartments site on Sibley Street). Fund 280 held $149,695 of pre-2011 redevelopment bond proceeds that SB 107 (2015) let the City use for housing; over $9.6 million was invested in multiple affordable projects after redevelopment dissolved in 2012.
affordability_requirement: Low and very low income housing per the original sources.
layering_notes: Recorded as negative information: Folsom's redevelopment successor housing money is essentially exhausted, so the City's capacity now rests on the in-lieu fee fund. Figures from the August 26, 2025 Housing Fund update staff report.

program_name: Rohnert Park affordable housing funds (Rental Affordable Housing Fee and Housing In-Lieu Fee account, Housing Fund) and Essential Housing Bond Financing Program (Housing Element Programs HO-3.F and bond program)
administering_agency: City of Rohnert Park Development Services Department and City Manager's office; City Council approves assistance
typical_award_size: No NOFA; the City provides gap loans or grants and land through development agreements and Council action, drawing on the segregated affordable housing fee account (budget Funds 4220 Affordable Housing Rental Fee and 4225 Affordable Linkage Fee) and the Housing Fund named in the 2023-2031 Housing Element as a funding source for Programs HO-1.B and HO-3.F (affordable housing on underutilized City sites, including extremely low income units). The Housing Element's Essential Housing Bond Financing Program commits the City to authorize CSCDA or another JPA to issue an estimated $191.3 million in governmental-purpose bonds for acquisition-conversion of market-rate apartments and new deed-restricted housing, forgoing about $337,346 in property tax and targeting at least 222 units (99 very low, 57 low, 66 moderate). Current fund balances and any adopted lending guidelines were not found; the City's budget and Housing Successor (LMIHAF) reports could not be located online.
affordability_requirement: Fee revenue must serve very low, low and moderate income households (Section 17.08.010(J)); bond program units for very low to moderate income; City-site projects target extremely low income units.
layering_notes: Rohnert Park was Prohousing designated August 4, 2023 (42 points), which gives projects in the city AHSC and IIG scoring preferences. Local money is thin, so the practical stack is County CFH, County PLHA (Rohnert Park is a non-entitlement city within the County PLHA), RED Housing Fund and County PBVs (county records) plus LIHTC, with the City contributing fee deferrals, land (Program HO-3.F) or a modest gap loan. Rohnert Park's former Community Development Commission was a redevelopment agency, so a Housing Successor LMIHAF may exist; no annual report was found (flag for follow-up). The CivicPlus agenda search on rpcity.ca.gov returned no results for affordable housing and the old rpcity.org pages 404, so recent council actions could not be verified. Source is the adopted 2023-2031 Housing Element on the City's DocumentCenter.

program_name: Irvine Community Land Trust (ICLT) land and development partnerships
administering_agency: Irvine Community Land Trust, 501(c)(3) created by the City of Irvine in 2006, 503 Nightmist, Irvine 92618; Board chaired by Ryan Aeh (2026)
typical_award_size: ICLT acquires or receives land (including City conveyances such as the four-acre site reported in the City's FY 2023-25 budget) and ground leases it to development partners so that units stay affordable permanently. Portfolio: Alegre Apartments, Doria Apartments, Parc Derian Apartments, Salerno Apartments (501 Nightmist) and Sage Park (affordable ownership); it reports hundreds of affordable units in Irvine and, since its 2017 mission expansion, elsewhere in Orange County. ICLT finances projects with LIHTC, HOME, Orange County Housing Finance Trust loans, FHLB AHP and HUD programs; dollar values of land contributions are not published.
affordability_requirement: Permanent affordability through recorded ground lease covenants; rental projects have served extremely low to low income households and Sage Park serves moderate income buyers.
layering_notes: ICLT is how Irvine converts inclusionary land dedications and City-owned parcels into 100% affordable projects without a city loan program; a developer partnering with ICLT gets site control at nominal ground rent and then stacks 4% or 9% credits, County MHSA/BHSA capital, OCHFT (Cypress Village Irvine took $3,500,000 in the 2024 OCHFT round) and OCHA PBVs. ICLT is a nonprofit, not a public agency, so its land alone does not trigger prevailing wage, but City land conveyed through it may. ICLT home, about, history, process, partnerships and properties pages and the September 23, 2026 letter opened on irvineclt.org.

program_name: City of Merced Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), 2019-2023 five-year plan (Resolutions 2021-113 and 2021-114)
administering_agency: City of Merced Housing Division (Fund 2018 Permanent Local Housing)
typical_award_size: About $3,112,314 over 2019-2023. The 2019 carryover ($518,719) and 2020 allocation ($806,250) went to Mercy Village (UPholdings and Self-Help Enterprises, 65 permanent supportive units on Park Avenue). 95% of 2021-2023 (about $1,608,830, including 2021 $887,254 and 2022 $444,694) is committed to Linc Housing's I Street project.
affordability_requirement: 55-year regulatory agreement. In Mercy Village the PLHA-restricted units are 6 at 30% AMI, 5 at 50% AMI and 11 at 60% AMI.
layering_notes: All current PLHA is spoken for, so a new project would depend on a future plan amendment or new allocations. The City has used PLHA as a matching layer for Homekey (Mercy Village) and 9% credits (I Street), alongside HOME and Housing Successor land. Merced County's own PLHA (county record) is separate and covers the unincorporated county.

program_name: Public Lands Unlocking Sites (PLUS) predevelopment guaranty program, LISC Bay Area
administering_agency: LISC Bay Area with a Chan Zuckerberg Initiative-backed guaranty
typical_award_size: $10 million guaranty that lets LISC provide predevelopment funding for affordable housing on surplus public land without borrower collateral; goal of over 800 affordable units by 2029 across 12 Northern California counties. Loan sizes and pricing are not posted.
affordability_requirement: Multifamily housing for households earning up to 80% AMI on surplus or public land.
layering_notes: Reclassified from other to loan: the guaranty is a credit enhancement that backs LISC Bay Area predevelopment funding to developers, so the deployable product is a predevelopment loan without borrower collateral (LISC lending products page; LISC 2023 Bay Area annual report). Designed for Surplus Land Act and other public-site dispositions where developers cannot pledge collateral before site control. Example cited: a 127-unit project on a 2-acre city and transit district site in Santa Cruz. Combine with BAHFA Priority Sites predevelopment loans and county or city surplus land programs. Public land involvement makes prevailing wage status project-specific.
